newsitem.title: CAMEROON: Cameroon sends in troops after unrest kills three.
newsitem.headline: Cameroon sends in troops after unrest kills three.

text.p: Cameroon sent troops to the southwestern town of Kumba on Wednesday after three opposition militants were gunned down in the aftermath of weekend elections, residents said.
The main opposition Social Democratic Front (SDF) said in a statement in the capital Yaounde that its three militants were killed on Tuesday.

They were shot dead "by thugs" loyal to local barons of President Paul Biya's ruling Cameroon People's Democratic Movement (RDPC), said the statement signed by SDF Secretary General Tazoacha Asonganyi.
The thugs "attacked the homes of SDF officials after officials at the election supervision commission refused to sign election returns showing the RDPC winning in Kumba," it said.

Residents contacted by telephone confirmed the deaths and said some of the attackers had been arrested. They said troops and gendarmes had been rushed in from the Southwest Province capital Buea and were patrolling streets of the tense town.
Kumba, 140 km (80 miles) southwest of Yaounde, is part of English-speaking Cameroon fiercely opposed to Biya's rule.
SDF won the Kumba municipal council in local elections in January 1996.
The government said on Wednesday a special commission headed by supreme court judge would go to work from Thursday to collate results of Saturday's legislative elections.
International observers said the elections, the second since the advent of multi-party politics in 1990, was tarnished by problems and irregularities.

But with opposition parties crying foul after the vote for a new 180-seat national assembly, the observers reserved judgment on whether or not the poll was free and fair. Formal results are not expected for over a week.
The capital Yaounde and the rest of the country were reported calm.
The nation's two main opposition parties, the SDF and the National Union for Democracy and Progress, have both called for results to be scrapped.
Both parties have urged their supporters to be prepared to defend their rights.

The Front's stronghold is the English-speaking North-West Province, a flashpoint in largely French-speaking Cameroon, but it also draws support from Cameroon's main ethnic Bamileke group and the urban poor.
